issues.legal_issue: A constitutional transfer of legislative authority over urban property ceilings does not displace State legislation governing tenancy and the conferral of occupancy rights.
material_facts: A State legislative resolution asked Parliament to regulate ceilings on urban immovable property, acquisition of property above the ceiling, and connected or incidental matters.
Tenants sought occupancy rights under the State land reforms law for land situated within an urban agglomeration.
Landowners challenged the occupancy-rights orders, arguing that the parliamentary ceiling law displaced the State law in its entirety.
issues.conclusion: The State law’s provisions governing tenancy and conferring occupancy rights remained applicable to the land; they did not conflict with the subject transferred to Parliament.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 246 and 252 and Entry 18 of List II, a resolution under Article 252 transfers only the distinct subject identified in the resolution, not the whole field of land legislation. The transfer concerned imposing ceilings on urban immovable property and acquiring property above those ceilings. Provisions regulating landlord-tenant relations and conferring occupancy rights are distinct matters within the State’s legislative competence, even if they have some effect on the subject assigned to Parliament. The Court relied on Union of India v. Valluri Basavaiah Chowdhary, Thumati Venkaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Calcutta Gas Company (Proprietary) Ltd. v. State of West Bengal, and Kannan Devan Hills Produce Company Ltd. v. State of Kerala.

issues.definition: When an occupancy-order challenge concerns urban-agglomeration land and the State provision governs tenancy or occupancy rather than imposing an urban-property ceiling, that State provision remains applicable.

issues.legal_issue: The State’s land-ceiling provisions do not govern the imposition of a ceiling on land within an urban agglomeration when that subject has been assigned to Parliament.
material_facts: The relevant State legislative resolution assigned Parliament the regulation of ceilings on urban immovable property and acquisition of property above those ceilings.
The land in question was within an urban agglomeration covered by the parliamentary ceiling law.
The State land-reform law also contained provisions imposing ceilings on landholdings.
issues.conclusion: For land within an urban agglomeration, the parliamentary ceiling law governs the imposition of the ceiling; the State law’s ceiling provisions do not apply to that extent.
issues.legal_principle: Article 252 permits Parliament to legislate on the distinct subject transferred by State resolutions, and the State legislature is denuded of competence over that transferred subject. The resolution transferred the imposition of ceilings on urban immovable property and related matters, not all subjects concerning land under Entry 18 of List II. The Court relied on Articles 246 and 252, Entry 18 of List II, and Thumati Venkaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh and Union of India v. Valluri Basavaiah Chowdhary.
